### 7.27 Owner-inactivity telemetry suspension (MYR-592)

> **Anchored:** FR-4.1 (vehicle enumeration), NFR-3.9 (data tiers), NFR-3.21 (self-scoped surfaces), NFR-3.28 (no raw telemetry persistence).

**Not an endpoint — a background policy**, documented here because it changes what §7.0 emits, what a phone buzzes about, and what a car does. It is the sibling of the §7.8 reservation sweeper and the `data-lifecycle.md` §5 pruning job: a periodic worker with product-visible consequences.

**Why it exists.** Tesla bills Fleet Telemetry streaming **per vehicle**. A car whose owner has stopped opening the app keeps streaming frames into a receiver nobody reads from, every day, for as long as the config lives — and the config's `exp` is **350 days**. The client's cost-control ruling:

| Owner silence | What happens |
|---|---|
| **≥ 4 days**, and this episode has not been warned | ONE push to the OWNER: *"{Car} will be disconnected tomorrow — open the app to keep it connected."* **Transactional, not preference-gated** (§7.19.4) |
| **≥ 5 days** | **SUSPEND**: remove the vehicle's fleet-telemetry config at Tesla, stamp `VehicleSummary.telemetrySuspendedAt` (§7.0). **No push** |

**Cadence:** hourly. That is a scheduling detail, not a product one — the thresholds are measured in days, so an hourly pass means a car crosses its threshold up to an hour late, which is invisible against a 24-hour notice period. Kill switch: `TELEMETRY_INACTIVITY_SUSPENSION_ENABLED`.

#### 7.27.1 What "activity" means, and whose

**An ACTIVITY is an ACCEPTED BEARER.** Every REST call and every WebSocket handshake resolves its token through one function, and that function stamps `go_user_activity.last_seen_at` for the subject. A real app open necessarily produces one. **A rejected token does not** — a forged bearer is not evidence its subject was around.

**THROTTLED to roughly one write per account-hour**, by an in-process gate plus an `ON CONFLICT … WHERE` guard in the statement itself. Unthrottled this would be the busiest write in the database (a WebSocket client revalidates continuously) in service of sub-second precision on a value compared against a **four-day** threshold. The stored value therefore lags reality by up to an hour, **always in the conservative direction**: a present owner reads as slightly less recent than they are, and the sweeper's response to "less recent" tops out at a warning a day before anything irreversible.

**STRICTLY THE OWNER'S ACTIVITY. This is an explicit client ruling and it is the rule most likely to be "fixed" by a later reader.** Rider and viewer usage of a shared car defers **nothing**. A car whose owner has been away five days is suspended while a rider is actively watching it. The platform pays for the stream on the OWNER's behalf and only the owner can decide to keep paying; the rider's honest rendering is the ordinary no-live-telemetry state (§7.0). The enforcement is structural rather than conditional — the candidate query joins the activity table on `"Vehicle"."userId"` **and nothing else**, so there is no rider probe to disable.

**EVERY ACCOUNT STAMPS; only owners' rows are ever read.** The writer does not ask whether the caller owns a car: the question costs a join on the hot path and its answer changes over an account's life. A rider's row is a few dozen bytes no sweeper query ever selects.

**AN OWNER WE HAVE NEVER OBSERVED IS NOT AN INACTIVE OWNER.** The join is INNER, so a vehicle becomes a candidate only once the platform holds positive evidence about its owner. An outer join would read a missing row as infinitely stale and **suspend the entire fleet on the first pass after deploy** — the single worst outcome available to this feature, made unreachable by construction rather than by a guard.

#### 7.27.2 What suspension touches — and what it must not

**ONE Tesla call**: `DELETE /api/1/vehicles/{vin}/fleet_telemetry_config`, the SAME call the §7.12 teardown makes, reused rather than re-implemented.

| Survives | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| The **OAuth grant** | Reconnecting needs no consent screen |
| The **virtual key** | Reconnecting needs no lock/unlock dance in the Tesla app |
| The **`Vehicle` row** | The car stays in the owner's catalog, dated rather than gone |
| Every **share** | A viewer's grant is untouched; they simply see a car with no live frames |
| Every **ride**, past and open | Nothing is cancelled and no ride table is written |

**A RIDE IN PROGRESS IS NOT SPECIAL-CASED, and that is the ruling.** An owner five days silent whose car is mid-ride is near-impossible and not quite — a shared rider can start one. There is deliberately no ride probe. What was verified is that the ride does not BREAK: suspension publishes no ride event, cancels nothing, ends no Live Activity and touches no ride table. The car stops sending frames, which every ride surface already tolerates as the ordinary offline case (the drive detector idles, the Live Activity holds its last state, the arrival flash does not fire). **The ride loses live frames and nothing else.**

#### 7.27.3 Episodes — warn once, and reset when the owner comes back

An **episode** is one continuous stretch of owner silence, recorded per vehicle in the Go-owned `go_vehicle_telemetry_suspensions` (migration **0044**) as two nullable instants, `warned_at` and `suspended_at`.

- **The warning fires ONCE per episode.** The mark is written **before** the push is published, deliberately: the event bus is fire-and-forget, so if the mark came second and failed, the next pass would warn again, and the one after that — twenty-four identical banners before suspension. In this order a failure loses at most one warning for one episode, and the in-app notice is still the backstop. **Spamming is the worse outcome and this order makes it impossible.**
- **Owner activity BEFORE suspension resets the episode** — the row is deleted, and the next absence starts from a clean warning. This runs as the sweeper's FIRST statement each pass, so a returned owner is never re-warned in the same pass they came back.
- **Owner activity AFTER suspension does NOT.** Only §7.28 reconnect clears a suspended episode. The config is gone at Tesla and no amount of app usage puts it back; auto-clearing the stamp would erase the disconnect notice while leaving the car just as silent.
- **Past BOTH thresholds with no warning on record → suspend, do not warn first.** A server down over an owner's fourth day wakes to a car past both. The THRESHOLD is what suspends, not the warning, and a notice issued at the moment of suspension is a notice with no notice period. `(warned_at NULL, suspended_at set)` is therefore an expressible and expected state.
- **An already-suspended vehicle is never re-examined.** It leaves the candidate set entirely, so it costs nothing per hour and cannot be warned again.

#### 7.27.4 Failure semantics — everything HOLDS

No failure advances a vehicle toward an irreversible action. Each arm below leaves the row untouched and lets the next hourly pass re-decide.

| Failure | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Episode-reset statement fails | **The whole pass holds.** Proceeding risks re-warning people who are demonstrably back — the noisiest failure this feature has |
| Candidate read fails | Pass holds |
| Owner's Tesla token unresolvable | **Hold before any Tesla call.** The truth is unknown and the next pass costs one lookup |
| Tesla config delete fails | Hold, **no stamp**. The delete is idempotent, so retrying is free |
| Config removed but the stamp fails | Hold. The catalog under-reports (the car reads connected while silent) until a later pass succeeds — indistinguishable from any offline car, and far better than the inverse |
| **No tesla-http-proxy configured** | The sweeper still WARNS but **never suspends**. Claiming a suspension we could not perform would tell every consumer a streaming, still-billing car is disconnected, behind a reconnect button that also cannot work. **Including past BOTH thresholds:** a car first observed already past day five on such a deploy is WARNED rather than held, because warning is the only thing that deploy can do and the alternative is that its owner never hears anything at all. Once per episode, exactly like every other warning |

**THE ORDER IS TESLA FIRST, STAMP SECOND**, and it is the same argument in both directions: stamping first would produce the one state the platform cannot explain to anybody — a catalog row saying "disconnected" for a car that is still streaming and still being billed, with an owner reading a disconnect notice while their live map updates behind it.

**Which cars are eligible.** There is no `telemetry_configured` boolean in the schema; the state is inferred from `go_fleet_config_attempts`, which is self-draining (the row is DELETED when a push succeeds — migration 0031). So a vehicle is treated as CONFIGURED unless a surviving schedule row carries a label meaning the push never took (`awaiting_virtual_key`, `push_failed`, `token_failed`, `read_failed`, `skipped_other`). The predicate is written as an exclusion on purpose: a car wrongly thought configured costs one idempotent Tesla DELETE and one warning about a car that was not streaming, while a car wrongly thought unconfigured **bills forever**, which is the entire failure this exists to prevent.

**Implementation:** [`internal/fleetsuspend`](../../internal/fleetsuspend) (the worker), [`internal/store/telemetry_suspension.go`](../../internal/store/telemetry_suspension.go) (episodes + the candidate query), [`internal/store/user_activity.go`](../../internal/store/user_activity.go) and [`internal/auth/user_activity.go`](../../internal/auth/user_activity.go) (the stamp), wiring `cmd/telemetry-server/wiring_fleet_suspend.go`.

---

### 7.28 `POST /api/tesla/vehicles/{vehicleId}/reconnect` (undo an inactivity suspension — MYR-592)

> **Anchored:** FR-4.1 (vehicle enumeration), NFR-3.21 (self-scoped surfaces).

Owner-authenticated "put my car back on" — the **RE-CONNECT** half of the two offers the §7.0 disconnect notice is required to carry (the other is the §7.12 unlink).

**Why this endpoint has to exist, and why it is so small.** §7.27's suspension removes exactly ONE thing: the vehicle's fleet-telemetry config at Tesla. So the way back is to put that one thing back, and nothing else. **There is no OAuth round trip, no consent screen, no lock/unlock dance and no re-pairing** — those belong to FIRST pairing (§7.11), and the fact that none of them is needed here is the whole justification for suspending as narrowly as §7.27 does.

**Enablement.** The route is **ALWAYS MOUNTED**, which runs opposite to the instinct its Tesla-touching siblings follow, and deliberately: it is the target of a link in the owner's disconnect notice, so a `404` would read as a broken app whereas the `502` an unconfigured proxy produces reads as "not right now" and is the truth. There is no risk in mounting it — with no pusher wired the handler refuses before it resolves a token, so no outbound Tesla call can fire from a proxy-less deployment or from CI.

**Request.**

```
POST /api/tesla/vehicles/{vehicleId}/reconnect
Authorization: Bearer <app session JWT>        # owner identity = JWT sub
```

`{vehicleId}` is the Prisma cuid (the same key as §7.12 / §7.14 — NOT a VIN). **No request body, and none is read**: there is one thing this endpoint does and no parameter could change it, so accepting a body would only create a shape to get wrong.

**Behavior / sequence:**

1. Validate the bearer → `userId`. Missing/invalid → `401 auth_failed`. Missing `{vehicleId}` → `400 invalid_request`. Non-`POST` → `405 invalid_request`.
2. Resolve `vehicleId` → (VIN, owner) via `VehicleRepo.GetByID`. Unknown vehicle → `404 not_found` (indistinguishable from ownership-filtered — never leaks existence). A real ownership mismatch → `403 vehicle_not_owned`. **Identical semantics to §7.12.** Neither writes anything and neither reaches Tesla. The distinction earns its keep here for the same reason it does on the §7.18 pause switch: a VIEWER holding the top `rides` tier reaches this endpoint legitimately authenticated and must still be refused — the suspension followed the OWNER's inactivity and the bill is theirs, so a rider restarting it would be spending somebody else's money. A car with **no VIN** never streamed and has no config to install → `409 conflict`.
3. Resolve the owner's Tesla token, **refreshing** it. The refreshing resolver rather than the stored one, deliberately: an owner four days silent has almost certainly let their access token expire. No linked Tesla account → `401 auth_failed` (the honest next step is re-linking, not retrying this call).
4. **Push the config** — the SAME call, the same `FleetAPIClient`, the same `EndpointConfig` and the same field map that first pairing uses, so what is re-installed is byte-identical to what the car was originally given.
5. **Clear the episode** — delete the `go_vehicle_telemetry_suspensions` row, both the suspension stamp and the warning bookkeeping, so the next absence starts clean.
6. Respond `200` with the resolved state.

**THE ORDER IS PUSH FIRST, CLEAR SECOND**, mirroring §7.27's delete-then-stamp for the mirror reason: clearing first would leave a catalog saying "connected" for a car with no config, an owner with no notice, and nothing left to press. In this order a failure leaves the suspension visible and the button live, which is exactly what somebody who just failed to reconnect should see.

**Idempotent (§4.5).** Calling it on a car that was never suspended re-pushes a config Tesla already holds and clears an episode that does not exist — both no-ops — and answers the same `200`. That is not tidiness: an owner who reconnects, background-refreshes and taps again must not be told their car is in a state it is not.

**No migration**, and no Prisma write of any kind. The episode row is Go-owned (migration 0044); CG-DL-9 does not apply because this ships no migration SQL at all.

**No WebSocket push.** A reconnect fires no `vehicle_update` frame. The catalog refreshes on its next read — and the car itself starts streaming again as soon as Tesla applies the config, which is the signal that actually matters.

**Response `200`** (`application/json`):

```json
{
  "vehicleId": "clxyz1234567890abcdef",
  "telemetrySuspendedAt": null
}
```

| Field | Type | Classification | Notes |
|-------|------|----------------|-------|
| `vehicleId` | `string` (cuid) | P0 | Echo of the path parameter. |
| `telemetrySuspendedAt` | `null` | P0 | Always `null` in a `200` body — the call would not have succeeded otherwise — and **emitted anyway, as an explicit null, rather than omitted**. It is the same key §7.0 carries and the same key the disconnect notice renders from, so a client can clear the notice through ONE code path instead of inferring the clear from an HTTP status. Same reasoning as the §7.18 echo: the client adopts the SERVER's answer. |

**Errors:**

| HTTP | `error.code` | When |
|------|--------------|------|
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Missing `{vehicleId}`. |
| 401 | `auth_failed` | Missing/malformed/invalid bearer; **or** no linked Tesla account (there is no grant to act under — re-link first). |
| 403 | `vehicle_not_owned` | Caller does not own the vehicle, including a `rides`-tier viewer (matches §7.12). |
| 404 | `not_found` | Unknown vehicle, or ownership-filtered — intentionally indistinguishable (matches §7.12). |
| 405 | `invalid_request` | Non-`POST` method. |
| 409 | `invalid_request` | The vehicle has **no VIN** and has never streamed; **or** Tesla accepted the request and **SKIPPED** the car (`vehicle skipped: missing_key`). The skip is the important one: it is not a server fault and **not retryable by tapping again** — the owner must re-pair the virtual key in the Tesla app — so it deliberately does not wear the `502` that invites a retry loop. Same status and same shape as the §7.10 fleet-config push returns for the same answer. |
| 500 | `internal_error` | The config was re-installed but the episode clear failed. **The Tesla side is already done**, so the retry is idempotent and cheap. |
| 502 | `internal_error` | Tesla or the proxy failed, or no fleet-config path is wired on this deployment. Retryable. Borrowed from the §7.10 push and §7.23 complete-setup rather than inventing a code. |

**No retry ladder.** The `FleetAPIClient` already retries 429s and 5xx internally; a second ladder here would turn somebody tapping a button into a long-running request they cannot cancel.

**Observability.** The success line carries the P0 `vehicle_id` / `user_id` and a **redacted** VIN (last 4). The owner's last-seen instant — the P1 behavioural value the suspension derived from — is never logged on this path or any other.

**Implementation:** [`internal/telemetry/vehicle_reconnect_handler.go`](../../internal/telemetry/vehicle_reconnect_handler.go) and `vehicle_reconnect_push.go`; wiring `cmd/telemetry-server/wiring_vehicle_reconnect.go`.

### 7.29 `POST /api/tesla/vehicles/{vehicleId}/acknowledge-owner-approval` (a driver states the owner approved adding the car — MYR-599)

> **Numbering, settled.** Contracts **v0.39.0** called this endpoint §7.24; **v0.40.0 corrected every citation to §7.29** and the corrected schemas are the ones vendored here. §7.24 in this document is and remains `POST /api/ride-requests/join` ([MYR-540](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-540)). See the numbering note below and **DV-25 (§10), now RESOLVED**.

> **Anchored:** FR-1.1 (vehicle telemetry), NFR-3.21 (ownership/authorization). Contracts **v0.39.0**, amended by **v0.40.0** (the §7.29 numbering, the §7.23 ownership-code sentence, and the new `owner_access_required` setup state). Request body `vehicle-setup-completion.schema.json#/$defs/AcknowledgeOwnerApprovalRequest`, response `VehicleSetupCompletionResponse`. Implemented by [MYR-599](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-599).

> **Numbering note, kept for the record now that it is settled.** Contracts v0.39.0's schema text cited this endpoint as **§7.24** in every place it named it (`vehicle-setup-completion.schema.json`, `vehicle-summary.schema.json`, `vehicle-state.schema.json`, and the `owner_vehicle_driver_access` hook's own header comment). **§7.24 in this document has been `POST /api/ride-requests/join` since 2026-08-13** ([MYR-540](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-540), contracts v0.35.0), so the endpoint was documented here at the next free number and the schemas' §7.24 was catalogued as **DV-25** (§10). **Contracts v0.40.0 corrected every citation to §7.29**, and the v0.40.0 schemas are the ones vendored in this repo, so the two now agree and DV-25 is RESOLVED. **The PATH is the contract; the section number is an index into this file.** Nothing in the wire shape, the request body, the response or the error set was ever affected by which number was used, which is why the vendored schemas were left byte-identical to the published package throughout rather than being locally patched — and it is why §7.24–§7.28 were never renumbered to free the number.

Bearer-authenticated *"yes, the owner said I could add this car"* — the consent gate in front of every fleet-telemetry config push at a vehicle its linker DRIVES but does not OWN.

**Why this endpoint has to exist.** [MYR-257](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-257) finding 3 put an **ownership filter** in the post-link provisioning hook: any Fleet API vehicle whose `access_type` was not `OWNER` was dropped with an `owner_vehicle_skipped reason=not_owner` audit line and nothing else. The intent was right and the mechanism was not — it conflated *"do not attach a car this person has no relationship with"* (which the token-scoped fleet listing and `UpsertOwnedVehicle`'s cross-user rule already guarantee, neither of which consults `access_type`) with *"do not act on a car this person does not own"*, which is the real concern. On **2026-09-05** a tester ran "Add another Tesla" for a car he drives on somebody else's Tesla account: OAuth completed, the token was stored, he paired the virtual key in the Tesla app — and no `Vehicle` row was ever created, so the app had nothing to show him and nothing to explain. **The filter was silent by design; the silence was the bug.** The client's ruling (Thomas, 2026-09-05) is that a driver MAY add the car, behind a pop-up in which they state the owner approved it. So the filter became **consent**: the car is provisioned, and **nothing is pushed at it** until this endpoint records the acknowledgment. This is the action half of that gate, exactly as §7.23 is the action half of `setupState`.

**What it records is EVIDENCE, not permission — and that distinction shapes everything below.** The platform cannot verify with Tesla that an owner approved anything; no Fleet API surface exposes such a fact. What it can hold is an attributable record that **this account, at this instant, was shown this version of this text and agreed**. That is what the platform would point to if an owner ever complained, and it is why the body carries a version id rather than a bare `{"confirmed": true}`: copy changes, and an acknowledgment that cannot name what was acknowledged is worth nothing.

**Enablement.** The route is **ALWAYS MOUNTED**, on §7.28's reasoning rather than §7.23's: it is the target of the only affordance a driver-linked car offers, so a `404` would read as a broken app. The endpoint's own work — one guarded `UPDATE` and one `AuditLog` insert — needs no Tesla call and no signing proxy at all. Only the config push that follows does, and that push is best-effort: on a deployment with no proxy the acknowledgment is still recorded and the response still carries an honest `setupState`.

**Request.**

```
POST /api/tesla/vehicles/{vehicleId}/acknowledge-owner-approval
Authorization: Bearer <app session JWT>        # caller identity = JWT sub
Content-Type: application/json

{ "acknowledgmentVersion": "owner-approval-v1" }
```

`{vehicleId}` is the Prisma cuid (the same key as §7.12 / §7.14 / §7.15 / §7.23 — NOT a VIN). Unlike its neighbours this endpoint **does** take a body, and the body is **strict**: `additionalProperties: false`, one required member, decoded with unknown fields refused.

| Field | Type | Required | Classification | Notes |
|-------|------|----------|----------------|-------|
| `acknowledgmentVersion` | `string`, 1–64 characters | **Yes** | P0 | **The version id of the acknowledgment text the client ACTUALLY RENDERED**, verbatim, on the sheet the person confirmed. The canonical text and its id ship with the contracts package — today `owner-approval-v1`, published as `docs/owner-approval-acknowledgment.md` — and a client MUST send the id of the copy it displayed and MUST NOT invent, abbreviate or re-word one. **THE SERVER DOES NOT VALIDATE IT AGAINST A LIST OF KNOWN VERSIONS, and that is deliberate:** an id this server does not recognise is still recorded exactly as sent, because a client shipped before a copy revision must not be blocked from finishing setup by a string comparison — the alternative fails the person in front of the sheet in order to protect a record about them. Format is a lowercase slug with a version suffix; treat it as an **opaque token** and never parse it for ordering. The server stores this string and the instant, and **nothing else** about the acknowledgment: no rendered copy (a published document with a stable id must not be duplicated per row), and no identity beyond the authenticated caller. |

**Behavior / sequence:**

1. Validate the bearer → `userId`. Missing/invalid → `401 auth_failed`. Missing `{vehicleId}` → `400 invalid_request`. Non-`POST` → `405 invalid_request`.
2. Decode the body strictly. A malformed body, a missing or empty-after-trim `acknowledgmentVersion`, one longer than 64 characters, or **any unknown field** → `400 invalid_request`. Nothing is written and no Tesla call is made.
3. Resolve `vehicleId` and confirm the caller owns the platform's `Vehicle` row. **Unknown vehicle *and* a real ownership mismatch both answer `404 not_found`** — see the divergence note below, because this is the one place this family of endpoints does NOT answer `403`.
4. **Record the acknowledgment, ONLY IF NOT ALREADY ACKNOWLEDGED.** `acknowledged_at` = now and `acknowledgment_version` = the id sent, written to the car's `go_vehicle_driver_access` row (migration **0046**) **in the same transaction** as an `AuditLog` row. **THE FIRST ACKNOWLEDGMENT WINS AND A LATER CALL NEVER OVERWRITES IT** — that first instant is the one the platform would point to if an owner complained, and a retry, a re-install or a second tap must not quietly move it forward.
5. **Owner-access car (no driver-access row):** nothing to acknowledge. Nothing is recorded, **no audit row is written**, and the call proceeds to step 6 — see "An owner's own car is a 200 no-op" below.
6. **Perform the SAME best-effort config push §7.23 performs**, on the car whose gate has just opened, and answer `200` with the vehicle's resulting `setupState`. The push is separable from the write on purpose: **a push that fails cannot roll back a consent that was genuinely given**, and the reconciler is already scheduled to repair the car.

**THE AUDIT ROW IS THE DURABLE HALF, and its metadata is exactly one key.** Action `vehicle.owner_approval_acknowledged`, `targetType` vehicle, `targetId` the vehicle's cuid, `userId` the acknowledging driver, metadata `{"version": "<the id sent>"}` **and nothing else** (CG-DL-5). There is deliberately **no VIN** (P1 — the target is already named by an opaque cuid), **no owner** (the platform cannot name them, and inventing a Tesla-side identity here would be a disclosure with no source), and **no rendered copy**. The standing `go_vehicle_driver_access` row is the GATE — "this car may now be configured" — and the audit row is the EVIDENCE — "this person agreed, then, to that". They are written together because a gate opened without evidence is the state nobody could later explain, and evidence for a gate that never opened is a record of a consent that had no effect. The row also **outlives the gate**: account deletion removes the driver-access row (§7.6 step **8f**, counted as `vehicleDriverAccessRowsDeleted`) and leaves the audit trail standing.

**OWNERSHIP FAILURE IS `404`, NEVER `403`, and this is a DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE from §7.23 / §7.15 / §7.12.** Those three answer `404 not_found` for an unknown vehicle and `403 vehicle_not_owned` for a real mismatch — a useful distinction on endpoints that read or actuate a car the caller may legitimately be a viewer of. **This endpoint records a CONSENT**, so the `403` arm would turn it into an existence oracle: a caller could enumerate cuids and learn which name real vehicles from the difference between the two codes, on the one surface whose whole subject is somebody else's property. The two arms are therefore collapsed, exactly as §4.1.1's silent-existence-hiding rule prescribes for surfaces where the distinction buys the caller nothing. **A client MUST NOT read `404` as "this vehicle does not exist"** — for this endpoint it means *"there is no vehicle here that you may acknowledge"*, which covers both cases and is all the caller is entitled to know.

> **A former contract/implementation divergence on §7.23 (DV-24, §10 — RESOLVED in contracts v0.40.0, which corrected the sentence rather than the code).** Contracts v0.39.0's schema text described this endpoint's ownership check as *"the SAME ownership check as §7.23 complete-setup, with the SAME answer when it fails: 404 `not_found`, never 403"*. **The ownership check is the same; the answer is not.** §7.23 answers `403 vehicle_not_owned` on a real mismatch, as its own error table has since MYR-505 and as §7.12 / §7.14 / §7.15 do. §7.29 is the divergent one **by design**, for the oracle reason above — it does not inherit `404` from §7.23, because §7.23 does not have it to give. Nothing here proposes changing §7.23: its `403` is correct for a surface whose caller may be a party to the car in some other capacity, and the schema sentence is the thing that is wrong.

**IDEMPOTENT (§4.5), and idempotent in the direction that matters.** A second call on an already-acknowledged car is a **`200`, never a `409`**. It re-runs the same best-effort push and returns the vehicle's current `setupState`, which makes it a safe retry for a client that lost the first response and a usable "try again" after a push that failed transiently. What it does **not** do is re-stamp the record. **THE FIRST ACKNOWLEDGMENT WINS, without exception** — the stored `acknowledged_at` and `acknowledgment_version` are the first ones and nothing moves them, not a retry, not a background re-sync, and **not a driver later confirming a *newer* version of the copy**. The instant a person first agreed is the thing the platform would point to if an owner ever complained, so a second call must not be able to re-date a months-old agreement as today's.

The statement behind this is `UPDATE … WHERE vehicle_id = $1 AND acknowledged_at IS NULL`, which makes the endpoint **self-debouncing**: a repeat matches zero rows, and *nothing at all* is written — not the columns, and **not a second audit row**, because one agreement recorded twice would misrepresent the trail this feature exists to produce. The push still runs on every call; only the record is written once. That also means the zero-row case covers **both** an already-acknowledged car and an owner-access car, which is convenient rather than accidental: both want identical behaviour, and neither is an error.

A **new copy version is therefore not recorded against an existing row.** If a future revision needs a second, independently-attributable consent, that is a new acknowledgment — the append-only AuditLog is the only surface shaped to hold more than one, and capturing it would be a deliberate change to this endpoint rather than a side effect of a client sending a different id.

**AN OWNER'S OWN CAR IS A `200` NO-OP, not an error.** A vehicle whose `teslaAccessType` is `"owner"` has no driver-access row and therefore nothing to acknowledge: nothing is recorded, **no audit row is written** (an audit trail that recorded non-events would be worse than useless in the one conversation it exists for), and the response carries the `setupState` the ordinary derivation yields. "This car needed no acknowledgment" is a fact about the car, not a fault of the request, so **a client that cannot tell the two cases apart is never punished for asking** — which is what lets a client offer the sheet from a stale row without first re-reading §7.0.

**FAILURE IS NEVER A STATE, exactly as on §7.23.** Every way this endpoint can fail is a typed HTTP error, and **no error response carries a `setupState` at all** — a client renders a retry affordance from the code rather than a setup card. The corollary is the one worth holding: a `200` here is never a claim that the car is now streaming, only that the gate is open and the server has done what it can with it.

**No new error code, no new sub-code.** Every code below is an existing member of the shared enum (§4.1.1).

**Response `200`** (`application/json`), contract [`schemas/vehicle-setup-completion.schema.json`](schemas/vehicle-setup-completion.schema.json) — **the SAME shape §7.23 returns**, deliberately, so a client reuses its existing completion handling verbatim rather than growing a second decoder for a second endpoint that answers the same question:

```json
{
  "vehicleId": "clmyr599driverlinked",
  "setupState": {
    "state": "awaiting_virtual_key",
    "since": "2026-09-05T11:07:12Z"
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Classification | Notes |
|-------|------|----------------|-------|
| `vehicleId` | `string` (cuid) | P0 | The Prisma cuid the request addressed, echoed so a client fanning several acknowledgments can attribute the answer. |
| `setupState` | `object` | P0 | **NEVER `null` on this surface**, exactly as on §7.23 and for the same reason: `null` means *no claim*, which is the honest answer to a passive read and useless as the answer to a request that just asked the server to unblock a car. Same two members and same semantics as `VehicleState.setupState`. |
| `setupState.state` | `string` enum | P0 | The **ordinary answer is the NEXT state, and as of contracts v0.40.0 that is `owner_access_required` for very nearly every real caller** — Tesla's `fleet_telemetry_config` POST is owner-only, so the acknowledgment is recorded and the push is refused in the same breath. `awaiting_virtual_key` (the driver has not paired a key yet, and the existing pairing card takes over) and `configuring` are what this call answers once Tesla permits a driver token to create a config — see §7.1's `owner_access_required` entry for why that may change without any change here — with `streaming` reachable on the §7.23-shared short-circuit for a car already sending frames, and `token_failed` when the linker's Tesla authorization can no longer be resolved. **`awaiting_owner_acknowledgment` is reachable here too, and means the acknowledgment did not stick** — the row was gone or the write did not apply — which is a state, not an error, and the client's correct response is to offer the sheet again. |
| `setupState.since` | `string` (RFC 3339, UTC) | P0 | When the evidence behind `state` was recorded. Never zero and never in the future — the server floors it at the read instant. Copy data, not a re-derivation input. |

**Errors:**

| HTTP | `error.code` | When |
|------|--------------|------|
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Missing `{vehicleId}`; a malformed or unparseable body; `acknowledgmentVersion` missing, empty after trimming, or longer than 64 characters; **or any unknown field** (strict decode). Nothing is recorded. |
| 401 | `auth_failed` | Missing/malformed/invalid bearer. **Note the asymmetry with §7.15, inherited from §7.23:** a caller whose *Tesla* token is unusable is NOT an auth failure here — the acknowledgment is still recorded and the answer is `200` with `setupState.state: "token_failed"`, because that is a setup condition the card already has copy for. |
| 404 | `not_found` | Unknown vehicle, **or** a real ownership mismatch — deliberately indistinguishable, and deliberately NOT the `403 vehicle_not_owned` §7.23 / §7.15 / §7.12 answer on the same input. See the divergence note above; this endpoint must not be usable to probe which vehicleIds exist. |
| 405 | `invalid_request` | Non-`POST` method. |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | REST rate limit breached (§4.1.2). There is no per-vehicle cooldown of §7.23's kind: the write is one guarded statement, and the push it triggers carries §7.23's own budgets. |
| 500 | `internal_error` | Store-layer failure recording the acknowledgment or its audit row. **The transaction is all-or-nothing** — a `500` here means neither the gate nor the evidence was written, so the retry is clean. |

**Observability.** VINs are redacted to last-4 in every log line (§9, CG-DC-2). The recorded version id is P0 and is logged; the copy itself never is, because the server never holds it. The provisioning-time counterpart of this event is the `owner_vehicle_driver_access` line the link hook emits (INFO, redacted VIN) — which **replaces** `owner_vehicle_skipped reason=not_owner` rather than adding a reason to it, since a car is now provisioned where one previously was not, and an operator reading the old event as "nothing happened" would be wrong.

#### Implementation

The store half is [`internal/store/vehicle_driver_access_write.go`](../../internal/store/vehicle_driver_access_write.go) — `VehicleRepo.AcknowledgeOwnerApproval`, which performs the guarded `UPDATE` and the `AuditLog` insert in one transaction and returns whether a driver-access row existed to stamp (the `false` that becomes this endpoint's owner-access no-op) — over the read projection and gate predicate in [`vehicle_driver_access.go`](../../internal/store/vehicle_driver_access.go). The `setupState` arm is MYR-491's derivation extended in [`internal/telemetry/vehicle_setup_state.go`](../../internal/telemetry/vehicle_setup_state.go), and the push it triggers is §7.23's, unforked. The gate this endpoint opens is consulted by the same driver-access row on every other push path — the reconciler's candidate query, `complete-setup`, `reconnect` and both fleet-config routes — so there is one fact and no second place to keep in step.

**Not in `specs/rest.openapi.yaml`, deliberately**, on §7.23's reasoning: that spec declares only the core read and sharing subset and carries **no `/api/tesla/*` path at all**. This endpoint's canonical machine-readable shape is [`schemas/vehicle-setup-completion.schema.json`](schemas/vehicle-setup-completion.schema.json) — `$defs.AcknowledgeOwnerApprovalRequest` for the request, `VehicleSetupCompletionResponse` for the `200`.

---

### 7.30 Trips — window-scoped live sharing (MYR-602)

> **Anchored:** FR-5.1 (sharing), FR-5.3 (revocation), FR-5.4 (roles), FR-3.2 / FR-9.1 (drive history), FR-9.3, NFR-3.21 (self-scoped surfaces), NFR-3.23 (location minimization). Contracts **v0.41.0**. Schemas [`trip.schema.json`](schemas/trip.schema.json). Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

Ten routes on one handler (nine from MYR-602, plus the owner's delete from [MYR-607](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-607)), and one sentence carries the feature: **a trip is a TIME WINDOW during which the share-holders an owner picked see the car's live location, its navigation, the window's drives and a per-leg Live Activity.**

**A trip creates NO new vehicle relationship.** Participants are chosen from the car's **already-accepted** `go_vehicle_shares` grants — that is where the picker's candidates come from — and the trip decides only what that existing grant *means between two instants*. The consequence is structural rather than procedural: **trip access can never outlive the share**, because every access query re-joins the live grant (`status = 'accepted' AND suspended_at IS NULL`) rather than trusting the participant row.

**ONE HANDLER TYPE serves all eleven**, and the same type also serves the two LEG token routes of **§7.21.7** (`/api/trip-legs/{legId}/activity-token`) — mounted here rather than beside the ride token routes because their authorization is a trip's and their kill switch is `TRIPS_ENABLED`. All thirteen share the same three things — the token validator, the store, and the 404-not-403 rule below — and thirteen constructors would be thirteen chances to wire one of them without the rule. The composition root is [`cmd/telemetry-server/wiring_trips.go`](../../cmd/telemetry-server/wiring_trips.go); the aggregate is `store.TripRepo` (migration **0047**), and its classification is [`data-classification.md`](data-classification.md) §1.25–§1.28. The architecture note is [`docs/architecture/trips.md`](../architecture/trips.md).

##### The 404-not-403 rule

**Every per-trip route answers `404 not_found` to a caller who is not on the trip, identically to how it answers for a trip that does not exist.** `GET`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `POST /end`, `GET /drives` and the token `POST` all take the same answer, and it is not a convenience: **trip ids are the kind of thing that ends up in a deep link** (`myrobotaxi://trips/{id}`), and a `403` would confirm that an id names a real trip. One answer for "no such trip", "somebody else's trip" and "a trip you have left" is what stops the surface being an oracle for trip ids.

**It is structural, not a per-handler branch.** The store resolves the caller's role IN THE SAME STATEMENT that reads the row (`tripRoleExpr` — `owner`, else `participant`, else `NULL`), and a `NULL` role becomes `ErrTripNotFound` at the scan. There is no read-then-authorize window, and no handler has a separate "are they allowed" branch that could answer differently.

**A participant getting `404` from `PATCH` is the one place the rule costs something in clarity**, and it is kept anyway. They can SEE the trip through `GET`, so a `404` from `PATCH` reads as odd. It is still the right answer: the alternative leaks nothing *here*, but it would make the surface's rule conditional — and a rule with one exception is a rule somebody applies inconsistently next time.

**`403 vehicle_not_owned` appears EXACTLY ONCE on this surface, on CREATE (§7.30.1)**, and that is not an inconsistency. The caller supplied a **vehicle** id, not a trip id, and a caller who can name a vehicle already knows it exists — they read it out of their own catalog. There is nothing left for a `404` to conceal. (An unknown `{vehicleId}` is still `404`, matching every other per-vehicle surface.)

##### The window and the derived status

**The window is `[startsAt, effectiveEnd)` — start INCLUSIVE, end EXCLUSIVE — where `effectiveEnd = min(endsAt, endedAt)`.** The predicate is spelled ONE way everywhere it appears (`starts_at <= NOW() AND NOW() < COALESCE(ended_at, ends_at)`): in `store.Trip.StatusAt`, in the wire projection's `tripStatusOf`, in the SQL status filter, in the catalog's `activeTripId` resolver, and character-for-character in `internal/auth`'s fourth UNION leg. **A surface that called a trip active while the access query called it over would render a live card over a socket that had already dropped the car.**

**`status` IS NEVER STORED.** It is computed from the clock on every read, and the reason is worth stating: **a stored status is the one state the platform could not explain** — a row saying `active` because a sweeper pass was missed, on a window that closed an hour ago. The sweeper's `started_notified_at` / `ended_notified_at` stamps record what was **NOTIFIED**, never what is **TRUE**; truth is always recomputed from the instants.

**`endedAt` and `endsAt` are separate facts and neither overwrites the other.** `endsAt` is the owner's **stated** window; `endedAt` is when they ended it early. Collapsing the two — writing the early end back over `endsAt` — would make an accidental "End trip" unexplainable afterwards, so the effective end is computed in every reader instead.

**A window MAY START IN THE PAST, and that is a designed capability rather than an oversight to guard against.** It is how the legs of a road trip **already driven** join the trip: the drive selection is WINDOW-based, not TAG-based, so nothing is written at drive time, a trip created after the fact picks up the drives already recorded, and extending a window backfills automatically. The validator deliberately does not check `startsAt` against now. **The 30-day cap** (`go_trips_window_capped`, and `store.MaxTripWindow`) is what stops a mistyped year handing out a decade of a standing live-location grant; on `PATCH` it is measured from `startsAt`, not from now.

##### What a trip ADDS over a share

**This is the product paragraph, and the delta is exact.**

An accepted **share** ([MYR-184](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-184)) buys a **catalog row** and, at the top tier (`allowRides`), the **right to request rides**. Since [MYR-369](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-369) it buys no drive history at all. **And since MYR-602 it no longer carries live location or navigation either** — §5's `viewer` narrowing withdrew both groups from a standing share, so a share on its own now answers *which car is this, can it make the trip, is it available* and nothing about where it is.

**A trip adds, for a bounded window and to a chosen subset of those share-holders:**

1. **The location and navigation groups** — the `trip_participant` mask role (§5.2.1), byte-for-byte the field set a `ride_member` holds, which is byte-for-byte the pre-MYR-602 viewer set. Live coordinates, heading, speed, the geocoded place strings, destination, ETA, route line, drive trail.
2. **`VehicleSummary.location`** on the catalog row (§5.2.0) — the coordinate the client's per-row pickup ETA is routed from.
3. **THE WINDOW'S DRIVES** — §7.2, §7.3 and §7.4, which are otherwise **owner-only since MYR-369**. This is the first and only non-owner drive read on the platform, and it is narrow: the drives inside a window the person was actually part of, and nothing else about the car's past.
4. **The per-leg Live Activity**, started by the server through the push-to-start token of §7.30.8 — because a leg begins when the CAR sets off, an event the phone learns from a push while the app is very likely not running, and ActivityKit does not let a background app start an Activity.
5. **The five `trips` pushes** — `trip_added`, `trip_started`, `trip_ended`, `trip_leg_started`, `trip_leg_arrived`.

**What a trip does NOT add:** a relationship. Remove the share and the trip grants nothing, immediately, on the next lookup, with no cleanup job in the path.

##### `activeTripId` on `VehicleSummary`

**`GET /api/vehicles` gains one optional field: the id of the trip whose window is OPEN on this car RIGHT NOW FOR THIS CALLER.**

**It exists because the wire `role` enum stays the closed two-member `owner | viewer`.** The server's resolution to `trip_participant` is invisible on the wire by design — installed builds switch on `role`, and a third member would change what an un-updated client does with a row it already understands — so **`activeTripId` is the ONLY thing that tells a non-owner client it may watch this car.** It is the trip-side counterpart of `hasActiveRide`. It is also the row's deep link: `myrobotaxi://trips/{activeTripId}`, and the same id fetches §7.30.3.

**ABSENT, NOT NULL, when there is no open window.** The contract marks the field optional; absence is what a pre-v0.41.0 server produces too, so a client that must handle absence anyway handles both. **A client MUST NOT read absence as "a trip may be running, we could not tell"** — the fail-closed reading is the correct one.

**On every role's allow-list, owner included** (§5.2.0), so an owner's own row can offer the trip card and the End-trip route; an owner is a party to their own trip. **P0** — an opaque cuid naming a relationship the caller is already party to, the tier of `role` and `sharePermission`. The resolving statement requires the caller to be the owner or a live participant holding a live share, so the field can never name a trip whose access the caller does not actually have.

**ONE TRIP AT A TIME PER VEHICLE, by construction:** overlapping scheduled-or-active windows on one car are refused at creation (`409 trip_overlaps`), so this is a single id and never a list.

**IT FLIPS ON ITS OWN, on BOTH edges, with no user action** — the window opens and closes on the clock. A client MUST re-read the catalog on the `trip_started` / `trip_ended` pushes rather than trusting a cached row. **REST-read-time only:** no `vehicle_update` frame carries it.

##### Kill switch `TRIPS_ENABLED`

Unset is ON. `TRIPS_ENABLED=false` makes **every one of the eleven routes — and the two §7.21.7 leg-token routes** — answer `503 service_unavailable`, reads included: a feature that can be switched off has to be switched off whole, and leaving `GET` alive would show an owner a live trip card whose every button returns an error. Anything `ParseBool` rejects **stops the process at boot** rather than being read as "off" — a typo that silently disabled a feature would be indistinguishable from an intentional shutdown.

**`503`, NOT `404`.** The routes are **always mounted**; the switch is passed INTO the handler rather than deciding whether to register. An unmounted route is a `404`, which tells a client the feature does not exist — and some clients cache that decision. A mounted route with the switch off says *"not right now"*, which is the true thing. The switch is also checked **before authentication**: when the feature is off the answer is the same for everybody, and there is no reason to validate a token to say so.

**⚠ IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT REVOKE LIVE ACCESS.** The four access legs in `internal/auth` read the trip tables directly and are **not gated by this switch**. Existing trips are not deleted, their windows are not closed, and participants keep the location group until their windows lapse. **A kill switch that silently dropped a participant mid-drive would be a data-availability incident dressed as a safety control.** To end access, **end the trips** (§7.30.5) — or delete them (§7.30.10), which ends access the same way and leaves nothing on anybody's list.

#### 7.30.1 `POST /api/vehicles/{vehicleId}/trips` — open a window

> **Anchored:** FR-5.1, FR-5.4, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. Request body [`trip.schema.json#/$defs/CreateTripRequest`](schemas/trip.schema.json), response `Trip`. Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose

The owner opens a window on their own car and admits people to it. **Owner only** — a share of any tier never lets somebody open a window on a car they do not own.

##### Request

```http
POST /api/vehicles/clvehicle0001/trips HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "vehicleId": "clvehicle0001",
  "name": "DFW → LA",
  "startsAt": "2026-09-06T14:00:00Z",
  "endsAt": "2026-09-09T02:00:00Z",
  "participantIds": ["clshare0001", "clshare0002"]
}
```

**`vehicleId` IN THE BODY IS IGNORED — THE PATH IS THE AUTHORITY.** `CreateTripRequest` carries the field and the server does not read it. A request whose body named a different car would otherwise have two answers to which car it is about; the schema keeps the field so the SDKs have one shape for the resource rather than a body that differs from the object it creates. **The two are not cross-checked and a mismatch is not an error** — the body's value is simply never consulted.

**Strict decode.** Unknown fields are refused (`400`), and the body is capped at **16 KiB** — generous by two orders of magnitude for a 60-character name and a list of share ids, and there so a malformed or hostile body is refused before it is parsed.

`participantIds` are **SHARE GRANT IDS** (`ShareInvite.inviteId` values for accepted grants), not user ids, and may be empty: an owner may open a window and add people later.

##### Response — 201 Created

The full `Trip` (see §7.30.3 for the shape), read back through the SAME view builder a subsequent `GET` uses — so a create response and the next read cannot disagree about the trip that was just made.

##### Validation

- **`name`**: trimmed, then **1 to 60 RUNES** (not bytes — a byte cap would refuse a 60-character name written in Japanese while accepting the same length in English), and no control characters. The identical function validates `PATCH`, so the two cannot drift.
- **The window**: `endsAt` strictly after `startsAt`, and at most **30 days** later. **`startsAt` may be in the past** and is deliberately unchecked. Both rules are stated TWICE — here and as `CHECK` constraints in migration 0047 — and the duplication is deliberate: the constraint is the one that cannot be bypassed by a future writer; this copy is what lets the API answer `400` with a sentence a person can act on rather than `500` with a constraint violation.
- **The participants**: every id must resolve to a **live, accepted, unsuspended** grant on **THIS** vehicle. **ALL OR NOTHING** — a create that silently dropped one invitee would produce a trip the owner believes has four people on it and that has three. The comparison is on **COUNTS**, never on which id fell out, so *"no such share"*, *"a share on somebody else's car"*, *"an invite never redeemed"* and *"a suspended grant"* are **one answer** (`400` + `participant_not_shared`): reporting which would make the endpoint an oracle for other people's share ids. **Duplicate ids collapse** rather than erroring.
- **The overlap**: another **scheduled-or-active** trip on the same vehicle covering any part of the window is `409` + `trip_overlaps`. **ENDED trips do not block** — history does not reserve the calendar, and since a window may start in the past a new one will routinely cover instants that old finished windows also covered.

##### Concurrency

**The whole create is ONE TRANSACTION**, because a trip that exists with an empty roster is worse than no trip: the owner sees a live window they believe they shared and nobody has access to it.

**The vehicle is ADVISORY-LOCKED before the overlap probe** (`pg_advisory_xact_lock` keyed on the vehicle), and that is what makes the overlap rule actually hold. The probe is a READ and the insert is a WRITE, so two concurrent creates on one car would both find no overlap and both commit — producing exactly the double window the `409` exists to prevent. The lock is transaction-scoped: released by the commit or the rollback, with nothing to clean up and no way to leak one, and it touches no other vehicle.

##### Pushes

`trip_added` goes to the participants (never the owner: a phone that buzzes to tell its owner about their own tap is the most common way a notification category gets turned off). **A create that lands INSIDE its own window** — the common case for a road trip already underway — additionally sends `trip_started` immediately, because the transition the sweeper would otherwise announce at the boundary is owed right now; the sweeper's `started_notified_at` stamp is what stops the two of them sending it twice. **Pushes happen AFTER the commit, never inside it:** a notification about a trip that then failed to save is the one failure mode worse than a trip nobody was told about.

#### 7.30.2 `GET /api/trips?status=&limit=` — the caller's trips

> **Anchored:** FR-5.4, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. Response [`trip.schema.json`](schemas/trip.schema.json) `TripListResponse`. Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose

Every trip the caller **owns** or is a **live participant** of, in one array, newest first. **ONE LIST FOR BOTH ROLES:** a trip the caller owns and a trip they were added to arrive in the same shape, and the sibling `role` on each row is the only thing that tells them apart.

##### Response — 200 OK

```json
{ "items": [ { "id": "cltrip0001", "role": "owner", "status": "active", "…": "…" } ] }
```

**⚠ THE ENVELOPE IS `{items: […]}` WITH NO CURSOR, AND THAT IS A CONTRACT STATEMENT RATHER THAN AN OMISSION.** This surface is **UNPAGINATED**. A person has a handful of trips, not a feed. It is deliberately **not** the `items` + `nextCursor` + `hasMore` envelope of the cursor-paginated lists (§7.2, §7.8), and **an SDK pagination helper MUST NOT mistake it for a page and go looking for a cursor that will never be there.** Consumers MUST NOT strip the envelope silently.

##### Validation

- **`status`** ∈ `scheduled` | `active` | `ended`, or absent for no filter. **An unrecognised value is `400`, not silently ignored.** A client that asked for `?status=activE` and received every trip would render the wrong list and never learn why; silently widening a filter is the failure mode a typed enum exists to prevent.
- **`limit`** is an integer in **[1, 100]**, default **50**. Out of range, or not an integer, is `400` — a bad `limit` gets a sentence rather than a silently clamped page.

**The status filter is evaluated in SQL, not in Go after the read**, because `limit` has to mean *"N trips of the requested status"*: filtering after the `LIMIT` would return a short page — or an empty one — while more matching trips sat behind it. The three SQL arms restate the window predicate and agree with `StatusAt` by inspection and by `TestTripStatusFilterAgreesWithStatusAt`.

**Ordering is `created_at DESC, id DESC`** — the same total order every other list in this codebase uses, so ties are stable. **⚠ A WORDING MISMATCH WITH THE VENDORED SCHEMA, recorded here rather than silently reconciled.** [`trip.schema.json`](schemas/trip.schema.json)'s `items` description says *"newest first (ORDER BY startsAt DESC, id DESC)"*; **the server orders by `created_at DESC, id DESC`.** Both are "newest first" and the two agree for every ordinary trip — one created now for a window starting now — and they diverge only for a **backfilling** trip, which is created today for a window that started last week and therefore sorts ahead of its `startsAt` neighbours here and behind them there. **The server's order is the correct one for this list**: it is the order every other list in this codebase uses, it is stable across ties, and it puts the trip the owner just made at the top, which is what a list of one's own trips is for. It is not catalogued as a DV because no client can observe a contract violation from it — the field the schema names is present and correct on every row, and the envelope declares no ordering guarantee a consumer may branch on. **A consumer MUST rely on "newest first" and MUST NOT re-derive the order from `startsAt`.**

**Rows are DECORATED PER ROW** — roster, vehicle, drive count, current leg — rather than in four batched queries. The list is capped at a hundred, so batching would buy microseconds and cost the property that a list row and a detail row are built by the same code and therefore cannot disagree. The cap exists to bound that decoration work, not the row count.

#### 7.30.3 `GET /api/trips/{tripId}` — one trip

> **Anchored:** FR-5.4, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. Response [`trip.schema.json#/$defs/Trip`](schemas/trip.schema.json). Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose

The trip as the caller sees it: the row, their relationship to it, and the four decorations the trip card renders. **Owner or live participant; `404` to everyone else** (see the 404-not-403 rule).

##### Response — 200 OK

```json
{
  "id": "cltrip0001",
  "vehicleId": "clvehicle0001",
  "name": "DFW → LA",
  "startsAt": "2026-09-06T14:00:00Z",
  "endsAt": "2026-09-09T02:00:00Z",
  "endedAt": null,
  "status": "active",
  "createdAt": "2026-09-05T22:41:03Z",
  "role": "owner",
  "ownerFirstName": "Nabil",
  "vehicle": { "vehicleId": "clvehicle0001", "name": "The Bus", "model": "Model Y", "year": 2024, "color": "UltraRed", "vinLast4": "8821", "trimLabel": "Long Range" },
  "participants": [ { "participantId": "clshare0001", "name": "Amruth", "userIsSelf": false, "addedByName": null } ],
  "driveCount": 14,
  "currentLeg": { "destinationName": "Barstow", "etaMinutes": 42, "startedAt": "2026-09-06T18:02:11Z" }
}
```

| Field | Type | Classification | Notes |
|-------|------|----------------|-------|
| `name` | `string` | **P1** | The owner's name for the trip. **USER CONTENT**, routinely naming a destination — sealed AES-256-GCM at rest as `name_enc` and **never logged, never placed in an error message** |
| `status` | enum | P0 | **DERIVED, never stored** — see the window block above. A consumer computing it itself MUST take `min(endsAt, endedAt)` and MUST treat an unrecognised member as `ended` (the safe direction) |
| `role` | `owner` \| `participant` | P0 | The CALLER's relationship, resolved in the same statement that read the row. **Deliberately NOT the same enum as `VehicleSummary.role`** (`owner` \| `viewer`) — the two answer different questions, and consumers MUST NOT alias them to one type |
| `ownerFirstName` | `string?` | P1 | The trip owner's **confirmed** first name, walking the same three-rung ladder and the same [MYR-583](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-583) confirmation gate as `VehicleSummary.ownerFirstName`. Keyed on the TRIP's owner rather than the vehicle's — **a car can change hands, and the card names the person whose trip it is** |
| `participants[]` | array | P1 (names) | The **LIVE** roster (`left_at IS NULL`), everybody except the owner. **Everyone on the trip sees the whole list** — they are on a trip together, and a road trip whose members cannot see each other is a group chat with the names blanked. `participantId` is the **SHARE** id, so the roster round-trips through `PATCH` without a second identifier. `name` follows the roster rule: the accepting account's confirmed **FIRST** name, else the owner's own label for the grant (an owner who invited "Mom" before she was through the naming prompt should see "Mom", not a blank row). **NO USER ID EVER REACHES THE WIRE** — it is compared against the caller to produce `userIsSelf` and then dropped, because publishing it would hand every participant a durable identifier for everybody else on the trip. Since [MYR-618](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-618) each row also carries **`addedByName`**: the CONFIRMED first name of whoever put this person on the trip, walking the same three-rung ladder and the same MYR-583 gate as `ownerFirstName`. **A NULLABLE KEY THAT IS ALWAYS PRESENT**, never absent, and `null` covers three causes deliberately collapsed into one — a row written before the attribution column existed, an adder who has not been through the naming prompt, and an adder whose account is gone. They mean the same thing to somebody reading a roster (there is nothing to show), and distinguishing them would disclose more about a third party than the row is entitled to. **EVERYONE ON THE TRIP SEES IT**, not only the owner, because since MYR-618 everyone on the trip can BE the answer — an attribution shown only to the owner would be a private ledger of who invited whom |
| `driveCount` | integer | P0 | Drives inside the window **as of this read**. Counted at read time like everything else about a window-scoped feature, so a trip created over a week already driven has a non-zero count the instant it exists, with nothing to backfill |
| `currentLeg` | object? | P1 (`destinationName`) | The driving leg underway, **ABSENT rather than null** when there is none — the one field on this shape where absence is the spelling. **INFORMATIONAL, NEVER A GATE:** a consumer MUST NOT condition its map, its live screen or its socket subscription on it. **An active trip with no leg is the ordinary overnight state, not a degraded one.** `etaMinutes` is read from the VEHICLE at REST-read time, not frozen at leg start: the leg records what the car set off toward, the vehicle carries how far away it is now. The leg is suppressed outright while the trip is not `active`, without asking the database — a leg left open past the end of a window must not render as "currently driving to Barstow" on a card that says ENDED |

The `vehicle` block is the catalog subset, carried inline so a participant's card needs no second call. `vinLast4` and the resolved `trimLabel` are produced by the **same helpers** §7.0 and §7.1 use, so the three surfaces cannot name one car three different ways.

**A trip name that will not decrypt renders EMPTY rather than failing the read**, and increments the decrypt-failure counter — the fail-soft posture every encrypted label in the store takes. A trip the owner cannot see is worse than a trip with a blank title, and the counter is what turns a wrong `ENCRYPTION_KEY` into a minutes-not-months detection.

#### 7.30.4 `PATCH /api/trips/{tripId}` — change the window or the roster

> **Anchored:** FR-5.1, FR-5.3, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. Request body [`trip.schema.json#/$defs/UpdateTripRequest`](schemas/trip.schema.json), response `Trip`. Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602), widened to participants by [MYR-618](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-618).

##### Purpose

Rename, move the scheduled close, add people, remove people. **THE OWNER MAY DO ALL FOUR. A LIVE PARTICIPANT MAY DO EXACTLY ONE — `addParticipantIds` — and nothing else** ([MYR-618](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-618)).

##### Who may send what

| Field | Owner | Live participant |
|-------|-------|------------------|
| `addParticipantIds` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `removeParticipantIds` | ✅ | ❌ `403 permission_denied` |
| `name` | ✅ | ❌ `403 permission_denied` |
| `endsAt` | ✅ | ❌ `403 permission_denied` |

**WHY THAT IS SAFE, and it is the whole argument: a trip MINTS NOTHING.** Its participants are drawn from the vehicle's already-accepted grants and from nowhere else, so the widest thing a participant can do is move somebody the OWNER already trusted with the car from *"sees it whenever the owner shares it"* to *"sees it during this window"*. They cannot invite a stranger, cannot create a grant, and the window they are widening is one the owner opened. Removing, renaming, moving the close, ending and deleting all stay with the owner.

**⚠ THE WHOLE REQUEST IS REFUSED AND NOTHING IS APPLIED** when a participant's body carries an owner-only field — **even alongside a perfectly legal `addParticipantIds`**. A partial apply is the worst of the three available answers: the client asked for two things, got a `200`, and one of them silently did not happen.

**PRESENCE, NOT VALUE.** `{"removeParticipantIds": []}` from a participant is `403`, because it is the client asking to exercise an owner's verb and the answer must not depend on whether the request happened to be a no-op — a rule that refused only the requests that would have DONE something is a rule nobody could state. An explicit JSON `null` is the one spelling that does not count: an absent key means UNCHANGED here, the owner's own path treats `{"name": null}` identically to omitting it, and the participant branch must not be stricter than the owner branch about a value that means nothing on either.

**⚠ THE ROLE IS RESOLVED BEFORE THE BODY IS INTERPRETED, and the order is the rule rather than an implementation detail.** A participant who sends `{"endsAt": "not-a-date"}` is told they may not move the window, **not** that their date is malformed: answering `400` would let them discover which fields this server validates and in what order, and it would also be the wrong sentence — the request was refused for what it asked to do, not for how it was spelled.

**`403` HERE, `404` EVERYWHERE ELSE, AND THAT IS NOT A CRACK IN THE 404-NOT-403 RULE.** That rule exists so a trip id cannot be probed. This caller has already been resolved as a member of this trip — they can read it through this same handler — so there is nothing left to conceal, and a `404` would only be a lie about a resource they are demonstrably on. **A caller who is on neither side of the trip still gets `404`, from the read, exactly as before.**

##### Request

```http
PATCH /api/trips/cltrip0001 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "endsAt": "2026-09-10T02:00:00Z", "addParticipantIds": ["clshare0003"], "removeParticipantIds": ["clshare0002"] }
```

Every member is optional and **absent means UNCHANGED** — the distinction the wire draws between an absent key and a present one survives all the way to the store rather than being flattened into a zero value. Strict decode and the same 16 KiB cap as §7.30.1.

##### Validation

**⚠ IT REFUSES OUTRIGHT ON AN ENDED TRIP: `409 conflict` + `trip_ended`.** Every mutation this offers is about a live window. Renaming a finished trip is pointless, adding somebody to one grants nothing, and **extending `endsAt` past NOW() on a lapsed trip would RESURRECT live access that every participant was already told had ended.** Continuing a road trip is a NEW trip, which says the true thing on everybody's phone. A bare `409` would be indistinguishable from a server bug and the client would retry; the sub-code is what lets it say the true thing instead.

**`endsAt` may SHORTEN to any instant ≥ now, or EXTEND within 30 days of `startsAt`.** A backwards `endsAt` — one in the past — is `400`, deliberately: it would end the trip **retroactively**, which is a different operation with a different name. **That operation is `POST /end` (§7.30.5), which stamps `endedAt` and leaves the owner's stated window intact so an accidental early end stays explainable.** Rejecting here is what keeps the two from being the same button.

**THE WHOLE WINDOW IS RE-VALIDATED, not just the field that moved.** A patch that only checked its own delta could walk a trip into a state no create would have accepted, one legal-looking step at a time. The overlap probe re-runs (under the same advisory lock, excluding the trip from its own probe so an extension does not collide with itself) whenever `endsAt` actually changes.

Added participants are resolved with the identical all-or-nothing, count-comparing rule as §7.30.1 (`400` + `participant_not_shared`) — **and the predicate does not soften because a participant is asking**: the target must be an accepted, unsuspended grant on THIS vehicle, so a suspended share is the same `400` for either caller. ([MYR-618](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-618) considered a `409` for the suspended case and kept the existing `400`: one condition must not answer two ways depending on who asked, which is exactly the drift this section's shared error table exists to prevent.) **A participant adding somebody already aboard is a no-op `200`** carrying the roster they asked for — it writes nothing, audits nothing, announces nothing, and succeeds, which is what the client meant. **ADDITIONS ARE APPLIED BEFORE REMOVALS**, so an id in both lists ends up **REMOVED** — the contract does not define that case, and the server picks the answer that grants less. Removing an id that names nobody on the trip is silently tolerated: it is the state the caller asked for, and erroring would make `PATCH` fail on a double-tap. **Re-adding somebody who left REVIVES their row** (`left_at = NULL`) and deliberately does NOT refresh `added_at`, which answers *"when did this person first join this trip"*.

##### Pushes

**Adding emits `trip_added` to the NEW ARRIVALS ONLY.** The handler reads the trip before the write purely so the fan-out can name them; sending to the whole roster on every patch would re-notify everybody already on the trip, which reads as the trip having been created a second time.

**WHEN A PARTICIPANT DID THE ADDING, THE OWNER ALSO HEARS `trip_participant_added`** ([MYR-618](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-618), §7.19.5) — *"Nabil added Joey to your trip"*, on the existing `trips` category with **no new preference**. It is the only push on this surface whose audience is the owner alone, and it exists because a participant's add is the one thing on the platform that changes who may watch an owner's car without the owner acting. **The OWNER's own add sends it to nobody**: a phone that buzzes to tell its owner about their own tap is the most common way a category gets switched off. The people just added hear the ordinary `trip_added` either way — what changed for them is identical whoever asked.

**The banner's names come from the roster the write read back**, already resolved by the roster's own rule (confirmed first name, else the owner's label for the grant), so the banner cannot call somebody one thing while the trip sheet one tap away calls them another.

**Removing emits NOTHING, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** The contract lists five `trips` events and **none of them is "you were removed"**. The person's live access ends the moment the row is stamped — the WS revalidator drops them, as it does for a revoked share — and announcing it would be telling somebody they have been taken off a trip by a person who chose not to tell them.

##### Audit

**One `trip.participant_added` AuditLog row PER PERSON ACTUALLY ADDED, written INSIDE the roster transaction** (CG-DL-3), for the owner's add and a participant's alike. `targetType='trip'`, `targetId`=the trip's cuid, **`userId`=THE ACTOR**, `initiator='user'`, `metadata={vehicleId, shareId}` — **three opaque cuids across the whole row and nothing else** (CG-DL-5).

**THE ACTOR IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE ROW.** Before MYR-618 only an owner could widen a roster, so *"who let this person see my car"* answered itself; now it does not, and the trip sheet's *"Added by {name}"* (`participants[].addedByName`, §7.30.3) is the same fact read from the roster's own attribution column rather than from an append-only log on a retention schedule.

**A no-op re-add writes nothing**, and **CREATE writes none of these rows**: a trip's initial roster is part of the act of creating it. **The added person's user id is deliberately not in the metadata** — the share id already names them to anybody who can read the vehicle's grants, and a user id would be a durable cross-surface identifier for a third party who is not the subject of the row. See [`data-lifecycle.md`](data-lifecycle.md) §4.2.

#### 7.30.5 `POST /api/trips/{tripId}/end` — end the window early

> **Anchored:** FR-5.3, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. No request body, response [`trip.schema.json#/$defs/Trip`](schemas/trip.schema.json). Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose

The owner closes the window now. **Owner only; `404` to everybody else, including a participant.**

##### Response — 200 OK, IDEMPOTENT

`200` rather than `204` because **the response carries the trip**, which is what tells the client the new `endedAt` and the now-`ended` status without a second call.

**⚠ IDEMPOTENT ALL THE WAY DOWN, and the guard is the point.** The statement is `UPDATE … WHERE id = $1 AND owner_user_id = $2 AND ended_at IS NULL`. A second call updates **zero rows**, the handler re-reads, and the endpoint answers `200` with the already-ended trip. **Re-stamping would move the end FORWARD on every retry — which, for an ACCESS boundary, means a double-tap silently extending somebody's live location by however long the two taps were apart.**

The trip is read **before** the write, so a trip the caller does not own answers `404` rather than producing a zero-row `UPDATE` indistinguishable from an idempotent repeat.

`trip_ended` is sent **only if the trip was live before the call**. Ending an already-ended trip must not re-announce it: the first call already told everybody, and a second announcement about the same fact is how a notification category gets turned off.

**The stated window survives.** `ends_at` is untouched; only `ended_at` is stamped, and every reader takes `min(endsAt, endedAt)`.

#### 7.30.6 `DELETE /api/trips/{tripId}/participants/me` — leave a trip

> **Anchored:** FR-5.3, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. No request body, no response body. Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose

The caller takes themselves off a trip. Live access ends on the next lookup — the access queries all carry `left_at IS NULL`.

##### Response — 204 No Content, ALWAYS

**⚠ SILENT AND IDEMPOTENT BY DESIGN. It reports NOTHING about whether the trip exists, whether the caller was ever on it, or whether they had already left, and it answers `204` in every one of those cases.**

A `404` for "not a member" would tell any authenticated caller which trip ids are real — exactly what the rest of this surface refuses to do — and **there is nothing a client would do differently with the distinction: it wanted to not be on the trip, and it is not on the trip.**

**AN OWNER CALLING IT IS A `204` NO-OP.** An owner holds no participant row, so there is nothing to stamp. Ending the trip is the operation they want and it has its own route (§7.30.5).

**A GENUINE TRANSPORT FAILURE IS STILL `500`.** `204` is the answer to *"you are not on this trip"*, **never** to *"the database is down"*. Answering `204` there would tell the caller they had left when they had not — and they would keep receiving the car's location.

The row is a **tombstone** (`left_at`), not a delete, so *"was this person ever on this trip?"* stays answerable and a later re-add is an `UPDATE` of one row rather than a second row for the same person.

#### 7.30.7 `GET /api/trips/{tripId}/drives?limit=&cursor=` — the window's drives

> **Anchored:** FR-3.2, FR-9.1, FR-9.2, NFR-3.21, NFR-3.23. Contracts **v0.41.0**. Response shape: **§7.2's `PaginatedDrives` envelope and §7.2's cursor encoding, verbatim** (declared inline in [`specs/rest.openapi.yaml`](specs/rest.openapi.yaml), like §7.2's own). Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose

**The FIRST surface on the platform that shows a non-owner a vehicle's drive history**, and the bound is the whole safety argument: a trip participant sees the drives of the window they were part of, and nothing else about the car's past.

##### Request

`?limit=` is an integer in **[1, 100]**, default **20** — §7.2's own bounds, from §7.2's own parser. `?cursor=` is §7.2's opaque base64-JSON keyset cursor, decoded by §7.2's own decoder. **A client can page a trip's drives with exactly the code it pages a car's drives with, and a cursor is not silently a different thing on the two surfaces.**

##### Response — 200 OK

`{ "items": [ DriveSummary… ], "nextCursor": string|null, "hasMore": boolean }` — the §7.2 envelope, with `nextCursor` anchored on the last item and `null` when there is no next page, built by §7.2's own encoder. Each row is projected through the **`trip_participant` mask** even though that mask is currently the identity over `DriveSummary`: running the projection anyway is what makes a future narrowing land here for free instead of silently not applying.

##### The window, and its ONE deliberate asymmetry

**The window is `[startsAt, effectiveEnd]` — INCLUSIVE AT BOTH ENDS — and it is resolved FROM THE TRIP, never from the request.** The handler passes a trip id and a user id; the store reads the window off the row it just authorized. **A parameterised window would let somebody on trip A read trip B's drives by supplying B's dates.**

**⚠ THE UPPER BOUND IS INCLUSIVE HERE WHERE THE ACCESS PREDICATE'S IS EXCLUSIVE, AND THE ASYMMETRY IS DELIBERATE.** They answer different questions. **Access** is about a live socket AT AN INSTANT: at exactly `effectiveEnd` the window is over and the frame must not be delivered, so `NOW() < COALESCE(ended_at, ends_at)` is half-open. **A DRIVE** is a thing that happened, and a drive that BEGAN exactly at the closing instant **is a drive of this trip** — excluding it would lose it from the only list it belongs to. The same inclusive bound is used by the drive count on §7.30.3 and by the §7.2/§7.3/§7.4 admission, so all four agree.

**The `startTime` bound is compared as an INSTANT, not as a string.** `Drive."startTime"` is a Prisma-owned TEXT column holding RFC 3339, and text ordering matches chronological ordering only while every row carries the same offset spelling. §7.2's cursor comparison already relies on that, and a wrong answer there is a pagination glitch; **here a wrong answer is an ACCESS DECISION** — a participant reading a drive from outside their window — so the bound is cast to `timestamptz`. The cursor comparison itself stays TEXT, byte-identical to §7.2's, so the two lists page the same way.

**Windows are ACTIVE **or** ENDED, never SCHEDULED**, on the §7.2/§7.3/§7.4 admission path — see §5.2.2. Live location is a window-scoped grant that ends with the window; the window's DRIVES are the record of a journey the person was part of, and having the list go dark the moment the trip ends would delete the feature at the exact moment it becomes worth reading. This endpoint reads ONE trip the caller is already on, so the same reasoning holds for it directly: a scheduled window simply contains no drives.

#### 7.30.8 `POST /api/trips/{tripId}/activity-start-token` — register the push-to-start token

> **Anchored:** FR-9.3, NFR-3.21. Contracts **v0.41.0**. Request body [`trip.schema.json#/$defs/RegisterTripActivityRequest`](schemas/trip.schema.json), no response body. Implemented by [MYR-602](https://linear.app/myrobotaxi/issue/MYR-602).

##### Purpose
